CT ‖ a_{k} = (1/T) ∫_{T} x(t) e^{−jkω_{o.title: Fourier series analysis (continuous time)
CT ‖ a_{k} = (1/T) ∫_{T} x(t) e^{−jkω_{o.about: Finds how much of each harmonic e^{jkω_{o}t} a periodic signal contains. Integrate over any one period; a_{0} is the signal's average value.
assumptions: x(t) is periodic with period T
Dirichlet conditions: x is absolutely integrable over a period, with finitely many extrema and discontinuities per period
At a jump the series converges to the midpoint
vars: complex amplitude of the k-th harmonic
related: synthesis: rebuild x from its coefficients

example.problem: Find a_{k} for x(t) = cos(ω_{o}t) + 2 sin(3ω_{o}t).
steps: Write each term with Euler: cos(ω_{o}t) = (1/2)e^{jω_{o}t} + (1/2)e^{−jω_{o}t}
Read off the coefficients (the integral gives the same): a_{±1} = 1/2, a_{3} = 1/j = −j, a_{−3} = j

DT ‖ a_{k} = (1/N) Σ_{n=<N>} x[n] e^{−jk.title: Fourier series analysis (discrete time)
DT ‖ a_{k} = (1/N) Σ_{n=<N>} x[n] e^{−jk.about: Finds the N coefficients of a periodic sequence by summing over any one period. Unlike the CT series there are only N distinct coefficients, and a_{k} repeats every N.
assumptions: x[n] is periodic with period N
The sum runs over any N consecutive n

example.problem: x[n] has period 4 with one period {1, 1, 0, 0} for n = 0..3. Find a_{1}.

CT ‖ x(t) = Σ_{k=−∞}^{∞} a_{k} e^{jkω_{o.title: Fourier series synthesis (continuous time)
CT ‖ x(t) = Σ_{k=−∞}^{∞} a_{k} e^{jkω_{o.about: Rebuilds a periodic signal as a sum of harmonics at multiples of the fundamental frequency, each weighted by its coefficient a_{k}.
assumptions: x(t) periodic with period T and satisfying the Dirichlet conditions
The infinite sum converges to x(t) where x is continuous and to the midpoint at a jump
For real x, a_{−k} = a_{k}^{*} and the pair of terms ±k add to a real cosine

example.problem: A signal of period T = 2π has a_{0} = 1, a_{±1} = 1/2 and no other coefficients. What is x(0) and x(π)?

DT ‖ x[n] = Σ_{k=<N>} a_{k} e^{jkω_{o}n}.title: Fourier series synthesis (discrete time)
DT ‖ x[n] = Σ_{k=<N>} a_{k} e^{jkω_{o}n}.about: Rebuilds a periodic sequence from its N coefficients. The sum is finite, so it is exact, with no convergence question.
assumptions: x[n] periodic with period N
Sum over any N consecutive values of k

x(t) = A_{0} + Σ_{k=1}^{∞} [A_{k} cos(kω.title: Trigonometric Fourier series
x(t) = A_{0} + Σ_{k=1}^{∞} [A_{k} cos(kω.about: The real-valued form of the Fourier series: a periodic real signal as its average plus cosines and sines at multiples of the fundamental.
assumptions: x(t) real and periodic with period T
Dirichlet conditions hold
Even signals have only cosines (B_{k} = 0); odd signals only sines (A_{0} = A_{k} = 0)

example.problem: A square wave of period T, +1 for the first half and −1 for the second (odd), has B_{k} = 4/(πk) for odd k and nothing else. Find the amplitude of its first three nonzero harmonics.
steps: A_{0} = 0 and A_{k} = 0 because the wave is odd with zero average

A_{0} = (1/T) ∫_{T} x(t) dt.title: DC term of the trig Fourier series
A_{0} = (1/T) ∫_{T} x(t) dt.about: The constant term is the signal's average over one period. It equals a_{0} in the exponential form. A common mistake is using 2/T as for A_{k} and B_{k}, which doubles the DC.
assumptions: x(t) periodic with period T
Integrate over any one full period
related: same number in the exponential form

example.problem: A pulse train is 5 V for 2 ms out of every 8 ms period and 0 V otherwise. Find A_{0}.
steps: A_{0} = (1/8 ms) ∫ over the period = (5 V × 2 ms)/(8 ms)

A_{k} = (2/T) ∫_{T} x(t) cos(kω_{o}t) dt.title: Cosine coefficients of the trig Fourier series
A_{k} = (2/T) ∫_{T} x(t) cos(kω_{o}t) dt.about: Projects the signal onto cos(kω_{o}t) to find the amplitude of the k-th cosine harmonic. The factor is 2/T, not 1/T, because a cosine's mean square is 1/2.
assumptions: x(t) real and periodic with period T
Zero for odd signals

example.problem: Find A_{1} for the even pulse train x(t) = 1 for |t| < T/4, 0 elsewhere in the period.

B_{k} = (2/T) ∫_{T} x(t) sin(kω_{o}t) dt.title: Sine coefficients of the trig Fourier series
B_{k} = (2/T) ∫_{T} x(t) sin(kω_{o}t) dt.about: Projects the signal onto sin(kω_{o}t) to find the amplitude of the k-th sine harmonic.
assumptions: x(t) real and periodic with period T
Zero for even signals

example.problem: Find B_{k} for the square wave that is +1 on (0, T/2) and −1 on (T/2, T).
steps: = 4/(kπ) for odd k, 0 for even k; B_{3} = 4/(3π) ≈ 0.424

a_{k} = (A_{k} − jB_{k})/2.title: Exponential coefficients from trig coefficients
a_{k} = (A_{k} − jB_{k})/2.about: Converts the real cosine and sine amplitudes of harmonic k into the complex exponential coefficient. The magnitude |a_{k}| is half the harmonic's amplitude.
assumptions: x(t) real
related: A_{k} = 2 Re a_{k}, B_{k} = −2 Im a_{k}

example.problem: Harmonic 2 of a real signal is 3 cos(2ω_{o}t) + 4 sin(2ω_{o}t). Find a_{2} and its magnitude.

a_{−k} = a_{k}^{*}.title: Conjugate symmetry of Fourier coefficients
a_{−k} = a_{k}^{*}.about: For a real signal the coefficient at −k is the complex conjugate of the one at +k, so |a_{k}| is even in k and ∠a_{k} is odd. You only need k ≥ 0.
assumptions: x(t) real-valued
If x is also even, a_{k} is real and even; if odd, a_{k} is imaginary and odd
related: the same symmetry for the Fourier transform

example.problem: A real signal has a_{3} = 2 − j. Find a_{−3}, and check the pair adds to a real signal.

x(t − t_{0}) ‖ a_{k} e^{−jkω_{o}t_{0}}.title: Time shift (Fourier series property)
x(t − t_{0}) ‖ a_{k} e^{−jkω_{o}t_{0}}.about: Delaying a periodic signal by t_{0} leaves each coefficient's magnitude alone and adds a phase of −kω_{o}t_{0}, linear in k.
assumptions: x(t) periodic with period T and coefficients a_{k}
Any real shift t_{0}

example.problem: x(t) has period T = 1 s and a_{1} = 1. Find the new a_{1} after delaying x by 0.25 s.

x(−t) ‖ a_{−k}.title: Time reversal (Fourier series property)
x(−t) ‖ a_{−k}.about: Reversing time turns each e^{jkω_{o}t} into e^{−jkω_{o}t}, so the coefficient at k moves to −k. A common mistake is negating the coefficients instead of swapping them; only an odd x gives a_{−k} = −a_{k}.
assumptions: x(t) periodic with coefficients a_{k}
For real x, a_{−k} = a_{k}^{*}, so reversal conjugates the coefficients
An even x has a_{−k} = a_{k}; an odd x has a_{−k} = −a_{k}
related: conjugation: for real x, reversal conjugates

example.problem: x(t) has a_{1} = 2j and a_{−1} = −2j (that is, x = −4 sin(ω_{o}t)). Find the coefficients of x(−t).
steps: So x(−t) = 4 sin(ω_{o}t), as sin is odd

dx/dt ‖ jkω_{o} a_{k}.title: Differentiation (Fourier series property)
dx/dt ‖ jkω_{o} a_{k}.about: Differentiating a periodic signal multiplies harmonic k by jkω_{o}: higher harmonics grow and the DC term disappears.
assumptions: x(t) periodic and differentiable (impulses allowed at jumps)
The derivative's a_{0} is 0

example.problem: x(t) = 3 cos(100t), so a_{±1} = 1.5 with ω_{o} = 100 rad/s. Find the coefficient of dx/dt at k = 1.

x(t) y(t) ‖ Σ_{l} a_{l} b_{k−l}.title: Multiplication (Fourier series property)
x(t) y(t) ‖ Σ_{l} a_{l} b_{k−l}.about: Multiplying the two series pairs harmonic l of x with harmonic k − l of y; their frequencies add to kω_{o}, so collecting terms gives this discrete convolution. A common mistake is multiplying coefficients a_{k}b_{k}; that is periodic convolution in time.
assumptions: x and y periodic with the same period T
a_{k} are x's coefficients and b_{k} are y's
related: ∫_{T} x(τ) y(t − τ) dτ ↔ T a_{k} b_{k}

example.problem: x = cos(ω_{o}t) has a_{±1} = 1/2. Find the coefficients of x^{2}.

(1/T) ∫_{T} |x(t)|^{2} dt ‖ Σ_{k} |a_{k}.title: Parseval's relation for Fourier series
(1/T) ∫_{T} |x(t)|^{2} dt ‖ Σ_{k} |a_{k}.about: The average power of a periodic signal equals the sum of the squared magnitudes of its coefficients, so each harmonic contributes |a_{k}|^{2} to the power.
assumptions: x(t) periodic with finite power
Sum over all integers k

example.problem: x(t) = 2 + 3 cos(ω_{o}t). Find its average power.

e^{jθ} = cos(θ) + j sin(θ).title: Euler's formula
e^{jθ} = cos(θ) + j sin(θ).about: Links the complex exponential to cosine and sine: e^{jθ} is the point at angle θ on the unit circle. Every polar-form and phasor calculation rests on it.
assumptions: θ real (it also holds for complex θ)
θ in radians: the series proof needs it
Why: put jθ into e^{x} = Σ x^{n}/n!; the even powers give the cos series and the odd powers give j times the sin series

example.problem: Write e^{j2π/3} in rectangular form.

e^{jθ} + e^{−jθ} = 2 cos(θ).title: Sum of conjugate exponentials
e^{jθ} + e^{−jθ} = 2 cos(θ).about: Adding e^{jθ} and its conjugate cancels the imaginary parts and leaves twice the cosine. This is why a real cosine has two spectral lines at ±ω.
assumptions: θ real

example.problem: Evaluate e^{jπ/3} + e^{−jπ/3}.

e^{jθ} − e^{−jθ} = 2j sin(θ).title: Difference of conjugate exponentials
e^{jθ} − e^{−jθ} = 2j sin(θ).about: e^{jθ} and e^{−jθ} are mirror-image phasors on the unit circle. Subtracting cancels their real parts (cos θ) and doubles the imaginary parts, leaving 2j sin θ. Divide by 2j to get sin θ.
assumptions: θ real (holds for complex θ too)
Common slip: dividing by 2 instead of 2j when solving for sin θ
related: the sum, which keeps the real parts

example.problem: Evaluate e^{jπ/6} − e^{−jπ/6}.

cos(θ) = (1/2) e^{jθ} + (1/2) e^{−jθ}.title: Cosine as complex exponentials
cos(θ) = (1/2) e^{jθ} + (1/2) e^{−jθ}.about: Splits a cosine into two counter-rotating phasors of half amplitude. Use it to find Fourier coefficients or transforms of sinusoids by inspection.
assumptions: θ real (holds for complex θ too)

example.problem: Find the Fourier series coefficients of 6 cos(4t + π/3).

sin(θ) = (1/2j) e^{jθ} − (1/2j) e^{−jθ}.title: Sine as complex exponentials
sin(θ) = (1/2j) e^{jθ} − (1/2j) e^{−jθ}.about: Solve e^{jθ} − e^{−jθ} = 2j sin θ for sin θ. A sine is two counter-rotating phasors with coefficients ±1/(2j) = ∓j/2, which is why a sine has a −j/2 at +ω and +j/2 at −ω in its spectrum.
assumptions: θ real (holds for complex θ too)
Common slip: 1/(2j) = −j/2, not j/2

example.problem: Find the Fourier series coefficients of 4 sin(10t).

(cos θ + j sin θ)^{n} = cos(nθ) + j sin(.title: De Moivre's theorem
(cos θ + j sin θ)^{n} = cos(nθ) + j sin(.about: Raising a unit complex number to a power multiplies its angle by the power. It follows from (e^{jθ})^{n} = e^{jnθ}.
assumptions: n an integer (for non-integer n the power has several values)

example.problem: Find (cos 30° + j sin 30°)^{6}.

cos^{2}(A) = 1/2 + (1/2) cos(2A).title: Cosine squared (power reduction)
cos^{2}(A) = 1/2 + (1/2) cos(2A).about: Turns a squared cosine into a constant plus a cosine at twice the frequency. Useful for average power and for squaring a sinusoid.
assumptions: Any angle A
Why: solve cos(2A) = 2cos^{2}(A) − 1 for cos^{2}(A)

example.problem: Find cos^{2}(π/8).

sin^{2}(A) = 1/2 − (1/2) cos(2A).title: Sine squared (power reduction)
sin^{2}(A) = 1/2 − (1/2) cos(2A).about: Turns a squared sine into a constant minus a cosine at twice the frequency; its average over a period is 1/2.
assumptions: Any angle A
Why: solve cos(2A) = 1 − 2sin^{2}(A) for sin^{2}(A)
Main use: ∫ sin^{2} x dx = x/2 − sin(2x)/4

example.problem: Find the average of sin^{2}(ωt) and sin^{2}(π/12).
steps: The cos(2ωt) term averages to 0, so the mean is 1/2

cos(A) cos(B) = (1/2)[cos(A − B) + cos(A.title: Product of cosines
cos(A) cos(B) = (1/2)[cos(A − B) + cos(A.about: Multiplying two sinusoids gives the difference and sum frequencies. This is the heart of mixing and AM modulation.
assumptions: Any angles A, B
Why: add cos(A − B) and cos(A + B); the sin·sin terms cancel and leave 2 cos A cos B
Common slip: the 1/2 in front, and which of A − B or A + B takes the minus

example.problem: A 1000 Hz tone is multiplied by a 100 kHz carrier. What frequencies come out, and what is cos(1)cos(2)?

sin(A) sin(B) = (1/2)[cos(A − B) − cos(A.title: Product of sines
sin(A) sin(B) = (1/2)[cos(A − B) − cos(A.about: Turns a product of sines into a difference of cosines at the difference and sum angles.
assumptions: Any angles A, B
Why: subtract cos(A + B) from cos(A − B); the cos·cos terms cancel and leave 2 sin A sin B
Common slip: the 1/2 in front, and which of A − B or A + B takes the minus

example.problem: Find sin(1) sin(2) with the identity.

sin(A) cos(B) = (1/2)[sin(A + B) + sin(A.title: Product of sine and cosine
sin(A) cos(B) = (1/2)[sin(A + B) + sin(A.about: Turns sine times cosine into a sum of sines at the sum and difference angles.
assumptions: Any angles A, B
Why: add sin(A + B) and sin(A − B); the cos·sin terms cancel and leave 2 sin A cos B
Common slip: the 1/2 in front, and which of A − B or A + B takes the minus

example.problem: Find sin(2) cos(1) with the identity.

cos(A) sin(B) = (1/2)[sin(A + B) − sin(A.title: Product of cosine and sine
cos(A) sin(B) = (1/2)[sin(A + B) − sin(A.about: Turns cosine times sine into a difference of sines at the sum and difference angles.
assumptions: Any angles A, B
Why: subtract sin(A − B) from sin(A + B); the sin·cos terms cancel and leave 2 cos A sin B
Common slip: the 1/2 in front, and which of A − B or A + B takes the minus

example.problem: Find cos(2) sin(1) with the identity.

e^{j0} = 1.title: Zero angle on the unit circle
e^{j0} = 1.about: A phasor with zero angle is the real number 1: no rotation, unit length.
assumptions: Angles in radians
Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: A phasor is 5e^{j0}. Write it in rectangular form.

e^{±j2π} = 1.title: A full turn on the unit circle
e^{±j2π} = 1.about: Rotating by a full turn in either direction brings you back to 1. This is why complex exponentials are periodic in angle with period 2π.
assumptions: Angles in radians
Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Simplify e^{j(π/3 + 2π)}.

e^{±jπ} = −1.title: Half a turn on the unit circle
e^{±jπ} = −1.about: A rotation of π either way lands on −1; e^{jπ} + 1 = 0 is Euler's identity. Multiplying by −1 is a 180° phase shift.
assumptions: Angles in radians
Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: A signal 4e^{j(ωt + π)} is how many times 4e^{jωt}?

e^{jπ/2} = j.title: Quarter turn counter-clockwise
e^{jπ/2} = j.about: Multiplying by j rotates a phasor 90° counter-clockwise. That is why an inductor's impedance jωL leads by 90°.
assumptions: Angles in radians
Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Rotate 3 + 4j by +90°.

e^{−jπ/2} = −j.title: Quarter turn clockwise
e^{−jπ/2} = −j.about: Multiplying by −j rotates a phasor 90° clockwise. A capacitor's impedance 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC) lags by 90°.
assumptions: Angles in radians
Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Rotate 3 + 4j by −90°.

e^{jπ/4} = (1 + j)/√2.title: 45° on the unit circle
e^{jπ/4} = (1 + j)/√2.about: At 45° the real and imaginary parts are equal, each 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071.
assumptions: Angles in radians
Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Write 10e^{jπ/4} in rectangular form.

e^{jπ/3} = (1 + j√3)/2.title: 60° on the unit circle
e^{jπ/3} = (1 + j√3)/2.about: At 60° the real part is 1/2 and the imaginary part √3/2 ≈ 0.866.
assumptions: Angles in radians
Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Write 2e^{jπ/3} in rectangular form.

e^{jπ/6} = (√3 + j)/2.title: 30° on the unit circle
e^{jπ/6} = (√3 + j)/2.about: At 30° the real part is √3/2 ≈ 0.866 and the imaginary part 1/2.
assumptions: Angles in radians
Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Write 4e^{jπ/6} in rectangular form.

e^{j0t} = 1.title: A zero-frequency exponential is constant
e^{j0t} = 1.about: A complex exponential at ω = 0 does not rotate; it is the constant 1 for all t. This is the DC term (k = 0) of a Fourier series.
assumptions: t real

example.problem: What is the k = 0 term of a Fourier series with a_{0} = 3?

e^{jπk} = e^{−jπk} = (−1)^{k}.title: Integer multiples of π
e^{jπk} = e^{−jπk} = (−1)^{k}.about: An integer number of half-turns alternates between +1 and −1. It shows up all over Fourier series and DT signals, for example e^{jπn} = (−1)^{n} is the fastest DT oscillation.
assumptions: k an integer

example.problem: Simplify e^{j3π} and e^{−j4π}.

e^{±j2πk} = 1.title: Integer multiples of a full turn
e^{±j2πk} = 1.about: Any whole number of full turns returns to 1. This makes DT frequencies repeat every 2π and DFT bins repeat every N.
assumptions: k an integer
related: DT frequencies are periodic, n an integer

example.problem: Show that e^{j(0.5 + 2π)n} = e^{j0.5n} for integer n, using n = 3.

j^{2} = −1.title: The imaginary unit squared
j^{2} = −1.about: The defining property of j (engineers use j because i is current). Use it to simplify every product of complex numbers.

example.problem: Multiply (2 + 3j)(4 − j).

1/j = −j.title: Reciprocal of j
1/j = −j.about: Dividing by j is the same as multiplying by −j, a 90° clockwise rotation. Handy for capacitor impedance and sine coefficients.
assumptions: Multiply top and bottom by j: 1/j = j/j^{2} = −j
Common slip: 1/j is not j; it rotates the other way

example.problem: Find the impedance of a 10 µF capacitor at ω = 1000 rad/s.

j = i.title: j and i are the same imaginary unit
j = i.about: Engineers write j for √(−1) because i means current; mathematicians write i. Q Calc accepts either.
assumptions: Both mean √(−1)

example.problem: Add 3 + 2i and 1 − 5j.
steps: Both units are the same, so add parts: (3 + 1) + (2 − 5)j

z = x + jy = r e^{jθ}.title: Rectangular and polar forms of a complex number
z = x + jy = r e^{jθ}.about: The same complex number written as real and imaginary parts, or as a magnitude and angle. Add in rectangular form; multiply and divide in polar.
assumptions: θ is defined up to multiples of 2π
related: x = r cos(θ), y = r sin(θ)

example.problem: Write z = −1 + j in polar form.

r = |z| = √(x^{2} + y^{2}).title: Magnitude of a complex number
r = |z| = √(x^{2} + y^{2}).about: The length of z from the origin, by Pythagoras. For a phasor it is the amplitude; for a transfer function it is the gain.
assumptions: x and y real
Common slip: including j in the square: |3 + 4j| = √(9 + 16), not √(9 − 16)

example.problem: Find |3 − 4j|.

θ = atan2(y, x).title: Angle of a point or complex number (atan2)
θ = atan2(y, x).about: The angle of the point (x, y), or of z = x + jy, measured counter-clockwise from the positive x (real) axis. atan2 uses the signs of both coordinates to pick the right quadrant, which atan(y/x) alone cannot.
assumptions: Result in (−π, π]
Undefined at the origin, x = y = 0
vars: angle from the +x axis (argument of z)
x coordinate, or the real part of z
y coordinate, or the imaginary part of z

example.problem: Find the angle of z = −3 − 3j.
steps: Third quadrant: atan(y/x) would wrongly give 45°

x = r cos(θ).title: x coordinate (real part) from polar form
x = r cos(θ).about: Projects a point at distance r and angle θ onto the x axis. For a complex number in polar form it gives the real part; for a phasor A∠φ it is the value of A cos(ωt + φ) at t = 0. Pair it with y = r sin(θ).
assumptions: θ measured counter-clockwise from the +x axis
θ in radians or degrees, consistently
vars: x coordinate, or the real part of z

example.problem: Find the real part of 10∠53.13°.

y = r sin(θ).title: y coordinate (imaginary part) from polar form
y = r sin(θ).about: Projects a point at distance r and angle θ onto the y axis. For a complex number in polar form it gives the imaginary part. Pair it with x = r cos(θ).
assumptions: θ measured counter-clockwise from the +x axis
θ in radians or degrees, consistently
vars: y coordinate, or the imaginary part of z

example.problem: Find the imaginary part of 10∠53.13°.

z_{1} z_{2} = r_{1} r_{2} e^{j(θ_{1} + θ.title: Multiplying in polar form
z_{1} z_{2} = r_{1} r_{2} e^{j(θ_{1} + θ.about: Magnitudes multiply and angles add, because e^{jθ_{1}} e^{jθ_{2}} = e^{j(θ_{1} + θ_{2})}. Cascading gains in a system works the same way: gains multiply, phase shifts add.
assumptions: Any complex numbers
Common slip: adding the magnitudes; they multiply

example.problem: Multiply 2e^{jπ/6} by 3e^{jπ/3}.

z_{1} / z_{2} = (r_{1}/r_{2}) e^{j(θ_{1}.title: Dividing in polar form
z_{1} / z_{2} = (r_{1}/r_{2}) e^{j(θ_{1}.about: Magnitudes divide and angles subtract. This is how you find a current from a voltage phasor and an impedance.
assumptions: Common slip: subtract the angles in the right order, numerator minus denominator

example.problem: A voltage 10∠30° V drives an impedance 5∠−30° Ω. Find the current.

z^{*} = x − jy = r e^{−jθ}.title: Complex conjugate
z^{*} = x − jy = r e^{−jθ}.about: Flips the sign of the imaginary part, mirroring z across the real axis. The magnitude stays; the angle changes sign.
assumptions: Any complex z
Picture: a mirror image across the real axis, same magnitude, angle negated

example.problem: Find the conjugate of 3 + 4j and of 2e^{jπ/5}.

z z^{*} = |z|^{2}.title: A number times its conjugate
z z^{*} = |z|^{2}.about: Gives the squared magnitude, a real number. Used to rationalise a complex denominator and to compute power |X|^{2}.
assumptions: Any complex z
Why: (x + jy)(x − jy) = x^{2} − j^{2}y^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}, always real and ≥ 0
Common slip: z^{2} is not |z|^{2} unless z is real

example.problem: Find 1/(3 + 4j) by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate.

Re z = (z + z^{*})/2.title: Real part from the conjugate
Re z = (z + z^{*})/2.about: Averaging z and its conjugate cancels the imaginary part. This is how a real signal A cos(ωt + φ) is Re{Ae^{jφ}e^{jωt}}.
assumptions: Any complex z
Common slip: dividing by 2j; that is the imaginary part's formula

example.problem: Find Re z for z = 2 − 7j.

Im z = (z − z^{*})/2j.title: Imaginary part from the conjugate
Im z = (z − z^{*})/2j.about: Subtracting the conjugate cancels the real part; dividing by 2j leaves the imaginary part as a real number.
assumptions: Any complex z
Im z is the real number y, not jy

example.problem: Find Im z for z = 2 − 7j.

Analysis ‖ X(jω) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} x(t) e^{−j.title: Continuous-time Fourier transform (analysis)
Analysis ‖ X(jω) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} x(t) e^{−j.about: Breaks an aperiodic signal into a continuum of frequencies. |X(jω)| says how much of frequency ω the signal holds and ∠X(jω) its phase.
assumptions: Exists in the ordinary sense if x is absolutely integrable, ∫|x(t)| dt < ∞
Signals like 1, u(t), cos(ω_{o}t) have transforms only with impulses δ(ω)
For real x, X(−jω) = X^{*}(jω)
related: from the Laplace transform, if the jω axis is in the ROC

example.problem: Find X(jω) for x(t) = e^{−2t}u(t), and its value at ω = 2 rad/s.

Synthesis ‖ x(t) = (1/2π) ∫_{−∞}^{∞} X(j.title: Inverse continuous-time Fourier transform (synthesis)
Synthesis ‖ x(t) = (1/2π) ∫_{−∞}^{∞} X(j.about: Rebuilds the signal from its spectrum as a weighted sum of e^{jωt} over all frequencies. The 1/2π comes from using ω in rad/s.
assumptions: X(jω) is the transform of x(t)
At a jump, the integral returns the midpoint
With f in Hz instead of ω, the 1/2π disappears

example.problem: X(jω) = 1 for |ω| < 10 rad/s and 0 elsewhere. Find x(0).

e^{−at} u(t), a > 0 ‖ 1/(a + jω).title: Decaying exponential and its transform
e^{−at} u(t), a > 0 ‖ 1/(a + jω).about: A one-sided exponential that starts at t = 0 and decays. Its transform is a first-order low-pass: flat below ω = a and falling 20 dB/decade above it. It is the impulse response of an RC circuit.
assumptions: a > 0 (real part positive) so the signal decays; for a ≤ 0 the integral diverges
Holds for complex a with Re a > 0

example.problem: An RC circuit with τ = RC = 1 ms has impulse response (1/τ)e^{−t/τ}u(t). Find |H| at ω = 1000 rad/s.

t e^{−at} u(t), a > 0 ‖ 1/(a + jω)^{2}.title: Ramped exponential and its transform
t e^{−at} u(t), a > 0 ‖ 1/(a + jω)^{2}.about: The exponential multiplied by t: it rises then decays, peaking at t = 1/a. Its transform is a double pole, the response of two identical first-order stages in cascade.
assumptions: Generally t^{n−1}e^{−at}u(t)/(n − 1)! ↔ 1/(a + jω)^{n}

example.problem: Find |X(jω)| for t e^{−3t}u(t) at ω = 4 rad/s.

δ(t) ‖ 1.title: Impulse and its transform (Fourier and Laplace)
δ(t) ‖ 1.about: A unit impulse contains every frequency equally: its Fourier transform is 1 at every ω, and its Laplace transform is 1 for every s. That is why a system's impulse response h(t) transforms to its frequency response H(jω), or its transfer function H(s).
assumptions: δ(t) is a generalised function with unit area at t = 0
Laplace: the lower limit is 0⁻, so the impulse at t = 0 is included; ROC is every s

example.problem: An impulse 3δ(t) enters a system. What is the input's spectrum at ω = 500 rad/s?

δ(t − t_{0}) ‖ e^{−jωt_{0}}.title: Delayed impulse and its transform
δ(t − t_{0}) ‖ e^{−jωt_{0}}.about: A shifted impulse has unit magnitude at all frequencies and a phase falling linearly with ω: a pure delay. A common mistake is e^{+jωt_{0}}: a delay always lags, so the phase is negative.
assumptions: Any real t_{0}

example.problem: Find the transform of δ(t − 2 ms) at ω = 250π rad/s.

1 ‖ 2πδ(ω).title: Constant (DC) signal and its transform
1 ‖ 2πδ(ω).about: A constant has all its energy at ω = 0, so its transform is an impulse there. It is not absolutely integrable (or summable), so the transform exists only in the generalised sense. The same pair holds for the constant sequence x[n] = 1 in the DTFT table, where the impulse repeats every 2π.
assumptions: Generalised (impulse) transform
DT: X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the table shows one period, and ω is in rad/sample

example.problem: Find the transform of x(t) = 5 V.
steps: An impulse of area 10π ≈ 31.4 at ω = 0

u(t) ‖ 1/(jω) + πδ(ω).title: Unit step and its transform
u(t) ‖ 1/(jω) + πδ(ω).about: The step is the integral of the impulse, so its transform is 1/(jω), plus an impulse for its average value of 1/2.
assumptions: Generalised transform: u(t) is not absolutely integrable
The πδ(ω) term carries the DC value 1/2

example.problem: Find the step's transform at ω = 4 rad/s.

e^{jω_{o}t} ‖ 2πδ(ω − ω_{o}).title: Complex exponential and its transform
e^{jω_{o}t} ‖ 2πδ(ω − ω_{o}).about: A single complex exponential is one spectral line at ω_{o}. Any periodic signal is a sum of these.
assumptions: Generalised transform
ω_{o} real
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: Find the transform of 3e^{j100t}.
steps: = 6πδ(ω − 100): one line of area 18.85 at ω = 100 rad/s

cos(ω_{o}t) ‖ πδ(ω − ω_{o}) + πδ(ω + ω_{.title: Cosine and its transform
cos(ω_{o}t) ‖ πδ(ω − ω_{o}) + πδ(ω + ω_{.about: A cosine is two complex exponentials, so it is two lines of area π at ±ω_{o}.
assumptions: Generalised transform
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: Find the transform of 4 cos(2π·60 t).

sin(ω_{o}t) ‖ (π/j)[δ(ω − ω_{o}) − δ(ω +.title: Sine and its transform
sin(ω_{o}t) ‖ (π/j)[δ(ω − ω_{o}) − δ(ω +.about: A sine is two lines at ±ω_{o} with imaginary areas −jπ and +jπ (π/j = −jπ).
assumptions: Generalised transform
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: Find the area of the line at +ω_{o} for 2 sin(ω_{o}t).

sin(Wt)/(πt) ‖ 1 for |ω| < W, 0 else.title: Sinc pulse and the ideal low-pass spectrum
sin(Wt)/(πt) ‖ 1 for |ω| < W, 0 else.about: A sinc in time is a rectangle in frequency. It is the impulse response of an ideal low-pass filter with cutoff W, which is non-causal and so only an ideal.
assumptions: At t = 0 the value is W/π (the limit)

example.problem: An ideal low-pass filter has cutoff W = 2π·1000 rad/s. Find its impulse response's peak h(0).
steps: h(0) = W/π (the area under H divided by 2π)

1 for |t| < T_{1}, 0 else ‖ 2 sin(ωT_{1}.title: Rectangular pulse and its transform
1 for |t| < T_{1}, 0 else ‖ 2 sin(ωT_{1}.about: A pulse of width 2T_{1} has a sinc-shaped spectrum with first zeros at ω = ±π/T_{1}. A shorter pulse spreads wider in frequency.
assumptions: At ω = 0, X = 2T_{1}, the pulse's area

example.problem: A pulse lasts from −1 ms to 1 ms. Find X at ω = 1000 rad/s and the first zero.
steps: First zero at ω = π/T_{1} = 3142 rad/s
example.answer: X(j1000) ≈ 1.683 × 10^{−3} s; first zero at 3142 rad/s

e^{−a|t|}, a > 0 ‖ 2a/(a^{2} + ω^{2}).title: Two-sided exponential and its transform
e^{−a|t|}, a > 0 ‖ 2a/(a^{2} + ω^{2}).about: A symmetric exponential decay has a real, even, Lorentzian spectrum. It is the sum of e^{−at}u(t) and its time reversal.

example.problem: Find X(jω) of e^{−2|t|} at ω = 2 rad/s.

e^{−t^{2}/(2σ^{2})} ‖ σ√(2π) e^{−σ^{2}ω^.title: Gaussian and its transform
e^{−t^{2}/(2σ^{2})} ‖ σ√(2π) e^{−σ^{2}ω^.about: A Gaussian transforms to a Gaussian. Its width in time is σ and in frequency 1/σ, the extreme of the time–bandwidth trade-off. A common mistake is thinking a wider pulse has a wider spectrum; the spectral width is 1/σ.

example.problem: For σ = 0.5 s, find X at ω = 2 rad/s.

Periodic p(t) with F.S. {ω_{o}, a_{k}} ‖.title: Transform of a periodic signal
Periodic p(t) with F.S. {ω_{o}, a_{k}} ‖.about: A periodic signal's transform is a train of impulses at the harmonics kω_{o}, each with area 2π times the Fourier series coefficient.
assumptions: p(t) periodic with a Fourier series
Generalised transform

example.problem: A periodic signal has Fourier coefficient a_{1} = −j/π. Find the area of its transform's impulse at ω = ω_{o}.

Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} δ(t − nT) ‖ (2π/T) Σ_{k=−∞}.title: Impulse train and its transform
Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} δ(t − nT) ‖ (2π/T) Σ_{k=−∞}.about: An impulse train with spacing T transforms to an impulse train with spacing 2π/T and area 2π/T. This is the basis of sampling: sampling in time repeats the spectrum every ω_{s} = 2π/T.
assumptions: Generalised transform

example.problem: Sample at 8 kHz. Find the spacing and area of the spectral impulses.
steps: Each impulse has area 2π/T, the same 50 265

d^{n}x(t)/dt^{n} ‖ (jω)^{n} X(jω).title: Differentiation (Fourier transform property)
d^{n}x(t)/dt^{n} ‖ (jω)^{n} X(jω).about: Each derivative multiplies the spectrum by jω, boosting high frequencies. It turns linear differential equations into algebra.
assumptions: x and its derivatives have transforms
n a positive integer

example.problem: Find H(jω) for dy/dt + 2y = x(t) and evaluate it at ω = 2 rad/s.

y(t) = x(t) ∗ h(t) ‖ Y(jω) = X(jω) H(jω).title: Convolution property
y(t) = x(t) ∗ h(t) ‖ Y(jω) = X(jω) H(jω).about: Convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency. An LTI system's output spectrum is the input spectrum times the frequency response.
assumptions: System is linear and time-invariant
X and H exist

example.problem: x(t) = cos(2t) enters H(jω) = 1/(1 + jω). Find the output's amplitude.
steps: A sinusoid comes out at the same frequency scaled by |H(j2)|

y(t) = x(t) p(t) ‖ Y(jω) = (1/2π) X(jω).title: Multiplication (modulation) property
y(t) = x(t) p(t) ‖ Y(jω) = (1/2π) X(jω).about: Multiplying two signals convolves their spectra (with 1/2π). Multiplying by a cosine shifts the spectrum to ±ω_{o}: amplitude modulation.
assumptions: Both transforms exist (possibly with impulses)

example.problem: A message band-limited to 5 kHz multiplies a 100 kHz carrier. What band does the product occupy?
steps: P(jω) has impulses at ±ω_{c}; convolving shifts X to ±100 kHz at half height

x(t − t_{0}) ‖ e^{−jωt_{0}} X(jω).title: Time shift (Fourier transform property)
x(t − t_{0}) ‖ e^{−jωt_{0}} X(jω).about: A delay leaves |X| unchanged and adds a phase −ωt_{0} that grows linearly with frequency.
assumptions: Any real t_{0}

example.problem: e^{−t}u(t) is delayed by 1 s. Find the transform at ω = 1 rad/s.
steps: |Y| = 0.707, same as before; only phase changed

e^{jω_{o}t} x(t) ‖ X(j(ω − ω_{o})).title: Frequency shift (Fourier transform property)
e^{jω_{o}t} x(t) ‖ X(j(ω − ω_{o})).about: e^{jω_{o}t} combines with e^{−jωt} in the analysis integral to make e^{−j(ω − ω_{o})t}, so X is read at ω − ω_{o}: the whole spectrum slides right by ω_{o}. Real modulation by cos does this both ways. A common mistake is shifting left; X(j(ω − ω_{o})) moves the spectrum to higher ω.
assumptions: Any real ω_{o}
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential
related: the dual: a delay is a phase ramp

example.problem: x(t) = e^{−t}u(t) times e^{j10t}. Find the new spectrum at ω = 10 rad/s.
example.answer: Y(j10) = 1, the old peak moved to ω = 10

x(at) ‖ (1/|a|) X(jω/a).title: Time scaling (Fourier transform property)
x(at) ‖ (1/|a|) X(jω/a).about: Compressing a signal in time (|a| > 1) stretches its spectrum and lowers it. Short pulses need wide bandwidth. A common mistake is writing X(jaω) or forgetting the 1/|a|.
assumptions: a real and nonzero; a negative also reverses time
related: a shorter pulse, a wider sinc

example.problem: x(t) = e^{−t}u(t) is played twice as fast, x(2t). Find its transform at ω = 2 rad/s.

x(−t) ‖ X(−jω).title: Time reversal (Fourier transform property)
x(−t) ‖ X(−jω).about: Flipping time flips frequency. For a real signal X(−jω) = X^{*}(jω), so the magnitude stays and the phase changes sign. A common mistake is X(−jω) = −X(jω); that holds only for an odd x.
assumptions: Any x with a transform

example.problem: Find the transform of e^{3t}u(−t) at ω = 4 rad/s.

t x(t) ‖ j dX(jω)/dω.title: Multiplication by t (frequency differentiation)
t x(t) ‖ j dX(jω)/dω.about: Differentiating the analysis integral with respect to ω brings down −jt, so j dX/dω is the transform of t x(t). It generates pairs like t e^{−at}u(t). A common mistake is the sign: it is +j dX/dω.
assumptions: X(jω) differentiable

example.problem: Derive the transform of t e^{−at}u(t), and evaluate it at a = 1, ω = 1 rad/s.

∫_{−∞}^{t} x(τ) dτ ‖ X(jω)/(jω) + πX(0)δ.title: Integration (Fourier transform property)
∫_{−∞}^{t} x(τ) dτ ‖ X(jω)/(jω) + πX(0)δ.about: The running integral is x convolved with u(t), so X is multiplied by the step's transform 1/(jω) + πδ(ω); the δ picks out X(0), the DC the integral keeps. Dividing by jω attenuates high frequencies. A common mistake is dropping πX(0)δ(ω) when x has nonzero area.
assumptions: The impulse term vanishes when X(0) = ∫x dt = 0

example.problem: Find the transform of (1 − e^{−t})u(t), the running integral of e^{−t}u(t), and its value at ω = 1 rad/s.

X(jt) ‖ 2πx(−ω).title: Duality
X(jt) ‖ 2πx(−ω).about: If x(t) ↔ X(jω), using X's shape as a time signal gives 2π times x's shape reversed in frequency. Every pair gives you a second pair for free.
assumptions: Swap the roles of t and ω

example.problem: Use e^{−|t|} ↔ 2/(1 + ω^{2}) to find the transform of 2/(1 + t^{2}), and its value at ω = 1.

∫ |x(t)|^{2} dt ‖ (1/2π) ∫ |X(jω)|^{2} d.title: Parseval's relation (CT Fourier transform)
∫ |x(t)|^{2} dt ‖ (1/2π) ∫ |X(jω)|^{2} d.about: Parseval: energy is the same whether summed in time or in frequency, because the transform only re-expresses x in another basis. |X(jω)|^{2}/2π is the energy density per rad/s. A common mistake is dropping the 1/2π when integrating over ω in rad/s (in hertz there is none).
assumptions: x has finite energy

example.problem: Find the energy of e^{−t}u(t) both ways.

Analysis ‖ X(e^{jω}) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} x[n].title: Discrete-time Fourier transform (analysis)
Analysis ‖ X(e^{jω}) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} x[n].about: Gives the spectrum of a sequence. It is periodic in ω with period 2π, and ω = π is the highest frequency a sequence can hold (half the sample rate).
assumptions: Converges if x is absolutely summable, Σ|x[n]| < ∞
Periodic and sinusoidal sequences need impulses
ω in rad/sample; physical frequency f = ωf_{s}/2π
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π
related: from the z-transform, if the unit circle is in the ROC

example.problem: Find X(e^{jω}) for x[n] = {1, 1} at n = 0, 1, and evaluate it at ω = π/2.

Synthesis ‖ x[n] = (1/2π) ∫_{2π} X(e^{jω.title: Inverse discrete-time Fourier transform (synthesis)
Synthesis ‖ x[n] = (1/2π) ∫_{2π} X(e^{jω.about: Rebuilds a sequence from one period of its spectrum. Because X is 2π-periodic, the integral runs over any interval of length 2π.
assumptions: X(e^{jω}) is the DTFT of x[n]
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: An ideal DT low-pass has H = 1 for |ω| < π/4. Find h[0].

a^{n} u[n], |a| < 1 ‖ 1/(1 − ae^{−jω}).title: Geometric sequence and its DTFT
a^{n} u[n], |a| < 1 ‖ 1/(1 − ae^{−jω}).about: A one-sided geometric sequence, the impulse response of a first-order recursive filter y[n] = ay[n − 1] + x[n]. 0 < a < 1 gives a low-pass; −1 < a < 0 a high-pass.
assumptions: |a| < 1 so the sum converges; for |a| ≥ 1 there is no DTFT
a may be complex with |a| < 1

example.problem: For h[n] = 0.5^{n}u[n], find |H| at ω = 0 and ω = π.
steps: A low-pass: gain 2 at DC, 0.667 at the highest frequency

(n + 1) a^{n} u[n], |a| < 1 ‖ 1/(1 − ae^.title: Ramped geometric sequence and its DTFT
(n + 1) a^{n} u[n], |a| < 1 ‖ 1/(1 − ae^.about: The DT counterpart of t e^{−at}u(t): a double pole, the response of two identical first-order stages in cascade. A common mistake is using n a^{n}u[n]; that one has ae^{−jω} on top.

example.problem: Find X at ω = 0 for a = 0.5, and check against the sum.

δ[n] ‖ 1.title: Unit sample and its transform (DTFT and z)
δ[n] ‖ 1.about: The unit sample has a flat spectrum: its DTFT is 1 at every ω and its z transform is 1 for every z. A filter's impulse response h[n] therefore transforms to its frequency response H(e^{jω}), or its transfer function H(z).
assumptions: δ[n] = 1 at n = 0, else 0
z transform ROC: the whole z-plane

example.problem: Find the DTFT of 4δ[n] at ω = π/3.

δ[n − n_{o}] ‖ e^{−jωn_{o}}.title: Delayed unit sample and its DTFT
δ[n − n_{o}] ‖ e^{−jωn_{o}}.about: A delay of n_{o} samples has unit gain and a linear phase −ωn_{o}. A common mistake is e^{+jωn_{o}}, which is an advance.
assumptions: n_{o} an integer

example.problem: Find the DTFT of δ[n − 2] at ω = π/4.

u[n] ‖ 1/(1 − e^{−jω}) + πδ(ω).title: Unit step sequence and its DTFT
u[n] ‖ 1/(1 − e^{−jω}) + πδ(ω).about: The step is a running sum of δ[n], so its DTFT is 1/(1 − e^{−jω}) plus an impulse for its DC value 1/2.
assumptions: Generalised transform: u[n] is not absolutely summable
X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the pair shows one period
related: Σ_{k≤n} x[k] ↔ X/(1 − e^{−jω}) + πX(e^{j0}) Σ δ(ω − 2πk)

example.problem: Find U(e^{jω}) at ω = π.

e^{jω_{o}n} ‖ 2πδ(ω − ω_{o}).title: DT complex exponential and its DTFT
e^{jω_{o}n} ‖ 2πδ(ω − ω_{o}).about: One spectral line at ω_{o}, repeated every 2π. Frequencies ω_{o} and ω_{o} + 2π give the same sequence.
assumptions: Generalised transform
X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the pair shows one period
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: Is e^{j(9π/4)n} different from e^{j(π/4)n}?
steps: They are the same sequence; check at n = 1: e^{j9π/4} = 0.7071 + 0.7071j

cos(ω_{o}n) ‖ πδ(ω − ω_{o}) + πδ(ω + ω_{.title: DT cosine and its DTFT
cos(ω_{o}n) ‖ πδ(ω − ω_{o}) + πδ(ω + ω_{.about: Two lines of area π at ±ω_{o} in each period. A DT cosine is periodic only if ω_{o}/2π is rational.
assumptions: Generalised transform
X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the pair shows one period
0 ≤ ω_{o} ≤ π for a unique frequency
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: A 1 kHz tone is sampled at 8 kHz. Where are its lines?

sin(ω_{o}n) ‖ (π/j)[δ(ω − ω_{o}) − δ(ω +.title: DT sine and its DTFT
sin(ω_{o}n) ‖ (π/j)[δ(ω − ω_{o}) − δ(ω +.about: sin(ω_{o}n) = (e^{jω_{o}n} − e^{−jω_{o}n})/(2j), and each exponential is one line of area 2π, so there are two lines at ±ω_{o} with areas −jπ and +jπ in each period. A common mistake is giving them real areas: the 1/j makes them imaginary and opposite in sign.
assumptions: Generalised transform
X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the pair shows one period
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: Find the area of the line at +ω_{o} for 3 sin(0.2πn).

sin(Wn)/(πn), 0 < W < π ‖ 1 for |ω| < W,.title: DT sinc and the ideal low-pass
sin(Wn)/(πn), 0 < W < π ‖ 1 for |ω| < W,.about: The impulse response of an ideal DT low-pass filter with cutoff W; truncated and windowed, it is the start of FIR filter design.
assumptions: 0 < W < π
At n = 0 the value is W/π
X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the pair shows one period

example.problem: Find h[0] and h[1] for an ideal low-pass with W = π/2.

1 for |n| ≤ N_{1}, 0 else ‖ sin(ω(N_{1}.title: DT rectangular pulse and its DTFT
1 for |n| ≤ N_{1}, 0 else ‖ sin(ω(N_{1}.about: A pulse of 2N_{1} + 1 ones has a periodic sinc (Dirichlet kernel) spectrum, equal to 2N_{1} + 1 at ω = 0 with zeros at multiples of 2π/(2N_{1} + 1).
assumptions: N_{1} a non-negative integer
At ω = 0 take the limit 2N_{1} + 1
vars: half-width of the pulse, in samples

example.problem: For N_{1} = 2 (five ones), find X at ω = π/2.

x[n − n_{o}] ‖ e^{−jωn_{o}} X(e^{jω}).title: Time shift (DTFT property)
x[n − n_{o}] ‖ e^{−jωn_{o}} X(e^{jω}).about: Delaying by n_{o} samples adds a linear phase −ωn_{o} and leaves |X| alone. A common mistake is e^{+jωn_{o}}: a delay lags.
assumptions: n_{o} an integer
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: x[n] = 0.5^{n}u[n] is delayed by 1. Find its DTFT at ω = π/2.

y[n] = x[n] ∗ h[n] ‖ Y(e^{jω}) = X(e^{jω.title: Convolution property (DTFT)
y[n] = x[n] ∗ h[n] ‖ Y(e^{jω}) = X(e^{jω.about: Each sample of h scales and delays x; the delays become e^{−jωk}, and summing them gives H(e^{jω})X(e^{jω}). So an LTI system multiplies the input spectrum by its frequency response. A common mistake is convolving the spectra: convolution in time multiplies them.
assumptions: System linear and shift-invariant
Transforms exist
related: y(t) = x(t) ∗ h(t) ↔ Y(jω) = X(jω) H(jω)

example.problem: A two-point average h = {0.5, 0.5} filters cos(πn/2). Find the output amplitude.

e^{jω_{o}n} x[n] ‖ X(e^{j(ω − ω_{o})}).title: Frequency shift (DTFT property)
e^{jω_{o}n} x[n] ‖ X(e^{j(ω − ω_{o})}).about: Multiplying by e^{jω_{o}n} slides the spectrum by ω_{o}. With ω_{o} = π, (−1)^{n}x[n] turns a low-pass into a high-pass.
assumptions: ω_{o} real
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential
DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: h[n] = 0.5^{n}u[n] is low-pass. Find the gain at ω = π of (−1)^{n}h[n].
steps: G(e^{jω}) = H(e^{j(ω − π)}); at ω = π it is H(e^{j0})

x[−n] ‖ X(e^{−jω}).title: Time reversal (DTFT property)
x[−n] ‖ X(e^{−jω}).about: Reversing a sequence reverses its spectrum; for real x it conjugates it. A common mistake is X(e^{−jω}) = −X(e^{jω}); that holds only for an odd x.
assumptions: Any x with a DTFT
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: Find the DTFT of 0.5^{−n}u[−n] at ω = π/2.

n x[n] ‖ j dX(e^{jω})/dω.title: Multiplication by n (DTFT property)
n x[n] ‖ j dX(e^{jω})/dω.about: Differentiating X(e^{jω}) = Σ x[n] e^{−jωn} with respect to ω brings down −jn; multiply by j to get the transform of n x[n]. A common mistake is the sign: it is +j dX/dω.
assumptions: X(e^{jω}) differentiable
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: Find the DTFT of n a^{n}u[n], and check it at a = 0.5, ω = 0.

x[n] − x[n − 1] ‖ (1 − e^{−jω}) X(e^{jω}.title: First difference (DTFT property)
x[n] − x[n − 1] ‖ (1 − e^{−jω}) X(e^{jω}.about: The delay gives e^{−jω}X, so the difference is (1 − e^{−jω})X. It is the DT stand-in for a derivative: a high-pass that blocks DC and doubles the highest frequency. A common mistake is treating it as jω exactly; that holds only for small ω.
assumptions: Any x with a DTFT
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: Find the first difference's gain at ω = 0, π/2 and π.

x[n] y[n] ‖ (1/2π) ∫_{2π} X(e^{jθ}) Y(e^.title: Multiplication (DTFT property)
x[n] y[n] ‖ (1/2π) ∫_{2π} X(e^{jθ}) Y(e^.about: Multiplying two sequences convolves their spectra periodically over one 2π period. Windowing a sequence smears its spectrum this way. A common mistake is multiplying the spectra; that is convolution in time.
assumptions: Both DTFTs exist
related: y[n] = x[n] ∗ h[n] ↔ Y(e^{jω}) = X(e^{jω}) H(e^{jω})

example.problem: x[n] is multiplied by cos(πn/2). Where does a spectral line of x at ω = 0.1 go?
steps: cos(πn/2) has lines at ±π/2 with area π; the (1/2π) gives half height

Σ_{n} |x[n]|^{2} ‖ (1/2π) ∫_{2π} |X(e^{j.title: Parseval's relation (DTFT)
Σ_{n} |x[n]|^{2} ‖ (1/2π) ∫_{2π} |X(e^{j.about: A sequence's energy equals the spectrum's energy averaged over one period. A common mistake is integrating over all ω; the DTFT repeats, so integrate over one 2π period only.
assumptions: x has finite energy
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: Find the energy of 0.5^{n}u[n].

Analysis ‖ X[k] = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} x[n] e^{.title: Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)
Analysis ‖ X[k] = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} x[n] e^{.about: Samples one period of the DTFT of an N-point sequence at the N frequencies ω_{k} = 2πk/N. The FFT computes it fast.
assumptions: x[n] has N points (pad with zeros for a finer frequency grid)
X[k] is periodic in k with period N
Bin k is the frequency kf_{s}/N

Synthesis ‖ x[n] = (1/N) Σ_{k=0}^{N−1} X.title: Inverse discrete Fourier transform
Synthesis ‖ x[n] = (1/N) Σ_{k=0}^{N−1} X.about: Rebuilds the N samples from the N DFT coefficients. The 1/N goes here in the usual convention.
assumptions: Treats x as one period of an N-periodic sequence

example.problem: A 4-point DFT is X = {10, −2 + 2j, −2, −2 − 2j}. Find x[0].

x(t) = A_{0} + Σ_{k=1}^{∞} C_{k} cos(kω_.title: Amplitude–phase (cosine) form of the Fourier series
x(t) = A_{0} + Σ_{k=1}^{∞} C_{k} cos(kω_.about: Writes each harmonic as one shifted cosine instead of a cosine plus a sine. C_{k} is the size of harmonic k and φ_{k} its phase, which is what a spectrum analyser shows.
assumptions: x(t) real and periodic

example.problem: Write x(t) = 3 cos(ω_{o}t) + 4 sin(ω_{o}t) in amplitude–phase form.

C_{k} = √(A_{k}^{2} + B_{k}^{2}) = 2|a_{.title: Harmonic amplitude of a Fourier series
C_{k} = √(A_{k}^{2} + B_{k}^{2}) = 2|a_{.about: The size of the kth harmonic, from the sine–cosine coefficients or from the exponential coefficient a_{k}. Plotting C_{k} against k gives the one-sided magnitude spectrum.
assumptions: k ≥ 1; the DC term is A_{0} = a_{0}, not doubled

example.problem: A square wave has a_{1} = 2/(jπ). How big is its fundamental?

φ_{k} = −atan2(B_{k}, A_{k}).title: Harmonic phase of a Fourier series
φ_{k} = −atan2(B_{k}, A_{k}).about: Expanding C_{k} cos(kω_{o}t + φ_{k}) gives A_{k} = C_{k} cos φ_{k} and B_{k} = −C_{k} sin φ_{k}, so φ_{k} = −atan2(B_{k}, A_{k}). It equals the angle of a_{k} = (A_{k} − jB_{k})/2. Common mistakes: atan(B/A) loses the quadrant when A_{k} < 0, and dropping the minus sign gives the sine-phase convention.
assumptions: φ_{k} is a cosine phase: a pure sine has φ = −π/2
Use atan2, not atan(B/A), so the quadrant is right when A_{k} < 0
related: same angle from the exponential form
the amplitude that goes with it

example.problem: Write −cos(ω_{o}t) + sin(ω_{o}t) as C_{1} cos(ω_{o}t + φ_{1}).
steps: φ_{1} = −atan2(1, −1) = −3π/4 ≈ −2.356 rad (atan(B/A) would give −π/4, the wrong quadrant)

B_{k} = 0.title: Even signals have only cosine terms
B_{k} = 0.about: If x(−t) = x(t), every sine coefficient vanishes, so only A_{0} and the A_{k} need computing. You can also integrate over half a period and double it. A common mistake is calling a wave even when it is symmetric about some other point; shift it so the symmetry is about t = 0 first, or sine terms remain.
assumptions: x even about t = 0

example.problem: Is a triangle wave centred on t = 0 made of sines or cosines?

A_{0} = A_{k} = 0.title: Odd signals have only sine terms
A_{0} = A_{k} = 0.about: If x(−t) = −x(t), the average and every cosine coefficient vanish, because the integral of an odd function over a symmetric period is zero; only the B_{k} are left. A common mistake is calling a wave with a DC offset odd: the offset brings A_{0} back.
assumptions: x odd about t = 0

example.problem: A square wave is +1 for 0 < t < T/2 and −1 for −T/2 < t < 0. Which coefficients survive, and what is B_{1}?
steps: x is odd, so A_{0} = A_{k} = 0
Even k give 0; odd k give 4/(kπ)
example.answer: sine terms only, odd k: B_{k} = 4/(kπ), B_{1} ≈ 1.273

A x(t) + B y(t) ‖ A a_{k} + B b_{k}.title: Linearity (Fourier series property)
A x(t) + B y(t) ‖ A a_{k} + B b_{k}.about: The analysis integral is linear, so it splits over a sum: the coefficients of a weighted sum are the same weighted sum of the coefficients. Build a signal from known pieces (a square wave plus a DC offset). A common mistake is adding signals of different periods; rewrite both over their common period first, which renumbers k.
assumptions: x and y share the period T
related: a x(t) + b y(t) ↔ a X(jω) + b Y(jω)

example.problem: x has a_{1} = 1/2 and y has b_{1} = −j. Find the k = 1 coefficient of 2x + 3y.

e^{jMω_{o}t} x(t) ‖ a_{k−M}.title: Frequency shift (Fourier series property)
e^{jMω_{o}t} x(t) ‖ a_{k−M}.about: Multiplying by e^{jMω_{o}t} adds M to every harmonic number, so each coefficient moves M places up the list: the new kth is the old (k − M)th. It is the series form of modulation. A common mistake is shifting the wrong way: a_{0} lands at k = M, not at k = −M.
assumptions: M an integer, so the period is unchanged
related: the dual: a time shift is a phase ramp

example.problem: x(t) = cos(ω_{o}t) has a_{±1} = 1/2. Find the coefficients of e^{jω_{o}t} cos(ω_{o}t).

x^{*}(t) ‖ a_{−k}^{*}.title: Conjugation (Fourier series property)
x^{*}(t) ‖ a_{−k}^{*}.about: Conjugating Σ a_{k} e^{jkω_{o}t} conjugates each a_{k} and turns e^{jkω_{o}t} into e^{−jkω_{o}t}, so the coefficient at index k comes from a_{−k}^{*}. For a real x, x = x^{*} gives a_{−k} = a_{k}^{*}. A common mistake is conjugating without mirroring the index.
assumptions: x(t) periodic with coefficients a_{k}

example.problem: x(t) = 2 + 3j e^{jω_{o}t}, so a_{0} = 2 and a_{1} = 3j. Find the coefficients of x^{*}(t).

∫_{−∞}^{t} x(τ) dτ ‖ a_{k}/(jkω_{o}).title: Integration (Fourier series property)
∫_{−∞}^{t} x(τ) dτ ‖ a_{k}/(jkω_{o}).about: Integrating e^{jkω_{o}t} gives e^{jkω_{o}t}/(jkω_{o}), so each coefficient is divided by jkω_{o}: high harmonics shrink, which is why a triangle wave (the integral of a square wave) looks smoother. It needs a_{0} = 0; otherwise the integral ramps and is not periodic. A common mistake is dividing a_{0} by zero; the new average is set by the constant of integration.
assumptions: a_{0} = 0 (zero average), or the integral grows without bound
The k = 0 coefficient of the result is its average, set by the constant of integration

example.problem: x(t) = cos(2πt) (T = 1 s, ω_{o} = 2π rad/s) has a_{±1} = 1/2. Find the coefficients of its integral.
steps: Check: ∫ cos(2πt) dt = sin(2πt)/(2π), whose c_{1} = 1/(2π · 2j) ✓

∫_{T} x(τ) y(t − τ) dτ ‖ T a_{k} b_{k}.title: Periodic convolution (Fourier series property)
∫_{T} x(τ) y(t − τ) dτ ‖ T a_{k} b_{k}.about: Convolving two signals of the same period over one period multiplies their coefficients (times T). It is the periodic counterpart of the convolution property, and it needs no transform with impulses. A common mistake is dropping the factor T.
assumptions: x and y share the period T
The integral runs over any one period
related: y(t) = x(t) ∗ h(t) ↔ Y(jω) = X(jω) H(jω)

example.problem: x and y both have a_{1} = b_{1} = 1/2 and T = 2 s. Find the k = 1 coefficient of their periodic convolution.

e^{jπ} + 1 = 0.title: Euler's identity
e^{jπ} + 1 = 0.about: Euler's formula at θ = π: walking half a turn (π radians) around the unit circle from 1 lands on −1. It links e, π, j, 1 and 0 in one line, and is the reason e^{jπk} = (−1)^{k}.
assumptions: π is in radians; e^{j180} is not −1

example.problem: Check it from Euler's formula.

cosh(x) = (e^{x} + e^{−x})/2.title: Hyperbolic cosine from exponentials
cosh(x) = (e^{x} + e^{−x})/2.about: The even part of e^{x}: average e^{x} and e^{−x}. It is never below 1, behaves like 1 + x^{2}/2 near 0, and is the shape of a hanging chain or cable (a catenary, y = a cosh(x/a)). It solves y″ = y with y′(0) = 0.
assumptions: Common slip: cosh^{2}(x) − sinh^{2}(x) = 1 has a minus
Even: cosh(−x) = cosh(x)

example.problem: A cable hangs as y = a cosh(x/a) with a = 50 m over a 40 m span. Find the sag at the middle.

sinh(x) = (e^{x} − e^{−x})/2.title: Hyperbolic sine from exponentials
sinh(x) = (e^{x} − e^{−x})/2.about: The odd part of e^{x}: any function splits into even and odd parts, and for e^{x} they are cosh and sinh, so e^{x} = cosh x + sinh x. It behaves like x for small x and like e^{x}/2 for large x. Hyperbolic sine solves y″ = y with y(0) = 0.
assumptions: Common slip: the identity is cosh^{2}(x) − sinh^{2}(x) = 1, with a minus, not a plus
Odd: sinh(−x) = −sinh(x); unbounded, unlike sin

example.problem: Find sinh(1) and check that cosh^{2} − sinh^{2} = 1.

cos(jx) = cosh(x).title: Cosine of an imaginary angle
cos(jx) = cosh(x).about: Putting θ = jx into cos(θ) = (e^{jθ} + e^{−jθ})/2 gives cosh. It is why hyperbolic functions turn up wherever damped or evanescent waves do.
assumptions: x real
Common slip: |cos z| ≤ 1 only for real z; cos(2j) is already 3.76

example.problem: Find cos(2j).

sin(jx) = j sinh(x).title: Sine of an imaginary angle
sin(jx) = j sinh(x).about: Put θ = jx into sin θ = (e^{jθ} − e^{−jθ})/(2j): e^{jθ} becomes the real e^{−x}, so the oscillation turns into exponential growth and the result is j sinh(x). Unlike sin of a real angle, it is not bounded by 1.
assumptions: x real; for a general complex angle, sin(x + jy) = sin x cosh y + j cos x sinh y
Common slip: |sin z| ≤ 1 only for real z

example.problem: Find sin(j).

cos(A ± B) = cos(A) cos(B) ∓ sin(A) sin(.title: Cosine of a sum or difference (angle addition)
cos(A ± B) = cos(A) cos(B) ∓ sin(A) sin(.about: From Euler: e^{j(A+B)} = e^{jA} e^{jB}; match the real parts and j·j = −1 supplies the minus. So the sign between the terms is opposite to the sign inside.
assumptions: Any angles A, B
Common slip: writing + for cos(A + B); it is cos cos minus sin sin
related: sin(A ± B) = sin(A) cos(B) ± cos(A) sin(B)

example.problem: Find cos(75°) exactly.

sin(A ± B) = sin(A) cos(B) ± cos(A) sin(.title: Sine of a sum or difference (angle addition)
sin(A ± B) = sin(A) cos(B) ± cos(A) sin(.about: From Euler: e^{j(A+B)} = e^{jA} e^{jB}. Expand both sides as cos + j sin, multiply out, and match the imaginary parts. The sign between the terms matches the sign inside.
assumptions: Any angles A, B
Common slip: sin(A + B) is not sin A + sin B
related: cos(A ± B) = cos(A) cos(B) ∓ sin(A) sin(B)
the real parts; its sign flips
a cos(θ) + b sin(θ) = R cos(θ − φ)

example.problem: Find sin(15°) exactly.

sin(2A) = 2 sin(A) cos(A).title: Double angle for sine
sin(2A) = 2 sin(A) cos(A).about: Set B = A in sin(A + B). Read backwards it turns a product sin·cos into one sine at twice the angle, which is why projectile range goes as sin 2θ and peaks at 45°.
assumptions: Any angle A
Common slip: sin 2A is not 2 sin A
related: sin(A ± B) = sin(A) cos(B) ± cos(A) sin(B)

example.problem: A ball leaves level ground at 20 m/s, 30° up. Its range is R = 2v^{2} sinθ cosθ/g = v^{2} sin(2θ)/g. Find R.

cos(2A) = cos^{2}(A) − sin^{2}(A).title: Double angle for cosine
cos(2A) = cos^{2}(A) − sin^{2}(A).about: Set B = A in cos(A + B). With sin^{2} + cos^{2} = 1 it also reads 2cos^{2}(A) − 1 or 1 − 2sin^{2}(A); pick the form that holds the function you know. Solved for cos^{2} or sin^{2}, it gives the power-reduction formulas used in integrals.
assumptions: Any angle A
Common slip: cos 2A is not 2 cos A
related: cos(A ± B) = cos(A) cos(B) ∓ sin(A) sin(B)

example.problem: Given cos A = 4/5 and sin A = 3/5, find cos 2A.

sin^{2}(A) + cos^{2}(A) = 1.title: Pythagorean identity
sin^{2}(A) + cos^{2}(A) = 1.about: The point (cos A, sin A) is on the unit circle, so by Pythagoras its coordinates' squares add to 1. Use it to get one of sin or cos from the other, or to swap sin^{2} for 1 − cos^{2} when simplifying.
assumptions: Any angle A
The square root loses the sign: pick it from the quadrant (cos is negative in quadrants II and III)
related: uses it for its other forms
the same Pythagoras with radius r

example.problem: sin A = 0.6 with A in the second quadrant. Find cos A.

a cos(θ) + b sin(θ) = R cos(θ − φ).title: Combining a cosine and a sine into one sinusoid
a cos(θ) + b sin(θ) = R cos(θ − φ).about: Any mix of cos and sin at the same frequency is a single shifted cosine with amplitude R = √(a² + b²) and phase φ = atan2(b, a). This is phasor addition and gives the peak of the sum.
assumptions: Why: expand R cos(θ − φ) = R cos φ cos θ + R sin φ sin θ and match: a = R cos φ, b = R sin φ
Common slip: φ = tan^{−1}(b/a) is wrong in quadrants II and III; use atan2(b, a)

example.problem: Write 3 cos(ωt) + 4 sin(ωt) as one cosine.

(a + jb)(c + jd) = (ac − bd) + j(ad + bc.title: Multiplying complex numbers in rectangular form
(a + jb)(c + jd) = (ac − bd) + j(ad + bc.about: Multiply out like any two binomials; the jb·jd term becomes j^{2}bd = −bd and moves into the real part. Quicker than polar when the numbers are given as x + jy; use polar for powers and chains of products.
assumptions: Any complex numbers
Common slip: +bd in the real part, from forgetting j^{2} = −1
vars: real and imaginary parts of the first
real and imaginary parts of the second
related: the same product in polar form

example.problem: A phasor current I = (2 + 3j) A flows through Z = (1 − j) Ω. Find V = I Z.

(a + jb)/(c + jd) = ((ac + bd) + j(bc −.title: Dividing complex numbers in rectangular form
(a + jb)/(c + jd) = ((ac + bd) + j(bc −.about: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate c − jd. The bottom becomes (c + jd)(c − jd) = c^{2} + d^{2}, a real number, and you can split the result into real and imaginary parts.
assumptions: c + jd ≠ 0
Common slip: dividing real by real and imaginary by imaginary; (a + jb)/(c + jd) is not a/c + j b/d

z^{n} = r^{n} e^{jnθ}.title: Powers of a complex number (de Moivre)
z^{n} = r^{n} e^{jnθ}.about: In polar form a power raises the magnitude to n and multiplies the angle by n. Far easier than expanding (x + jy)^{n}.
assumptions: n an integer; for fractional n see z^{1/n}, which has n roots
θ in radians; reduce nθ by multiples of 2π at the end
related: (cos θ + j sin θ)^{n} = cos(nθ) + j sin(nθ)

z^{1/n} = r^{1/n} e^{j(θ + 2πk)/n}.title: nth roots of a complex number
z^{1/n} = r^{1/n} e^{j(θ + 2πk)/n}.about: A nonzero number has exactly n nth roots, equally spaced around a circle of radius r^{1/n}. Step k from 0 to n − 1.
assumptions: k = 0 gives the principal root; k = n repeats k = 0
There are n distinct roots, k = 0, 1, …, n − 1, evenly spaced 2π/n apart on a circle
Common slip: stopping at k = 0, the principal root
related: why adding 2πk changes nothing in z but gives new roots

example.problem: Find the cube roots of 8.

ln z = ln r + j(θ + 2πk).title: Logarithm of a complex number
ln z = ln r + j(θ + 2πk).about: Take the log of the magnitude for the real part; the angle becomes the imaginary part. It has many values, 2π apart; k = 0 with −π < θ ≤ π is the principal one.
assumptions: k = 0 with −π < θ ≤ π gives the principal value
Common slip: ln is many-valued; a calculator gives only the principal value, −π < θ ≤ π, k = 0

example.problem: Find the principal value of ln(−1).

|z_{1} + z_{2}| ≤ |z_{1}| + |z_{2}|.title: Triangle inequality
|z_{1} + z_{2}| ≤ |z_{1}| + |z_{2}|.about: Adding complex numbers adds arrows tip to tail, so the sum is never longer than the two lengths together. Equality holds when they point the same way.
assumptions: Any complex numbers (or 2D vectors)
Equality only when z_{1} and z_{2} point the same way
Why: the third side of a triangle is never longer than the other two together; equality when z_{1} and z_{2} point the same way

example.problem: Check it for z_{1} = 3 and z_{2} = 4j.

sgn(t) ‖ 2/(jω).title: Sign function and its transform
sgn(t) ‖ 2/(jω).about: sgn(t) is −1 for t < 0 and +1 for t > 0. Its transform has no DC impulse because its average is zero; u(t) = (1 + sgn(t))/2 gives the step's transform from it.
assumptions: Generalised transform: sgn(t) is not absolutely integrable
sgn(0) = 0; a value at a single instant doesn't change the transform
Purely imaginary and odd, since sgn is real and odd
vars: sign function: −1 for t < 0, +1 for t > 0

example.problem: Get the step's transform from this pair, and evaluate sgn's transform at ω = 4 rad/s.

t^{n−1} e^{−at} u(t)/(n − 1)!, a > 0 ‖ 1.title: Repeated-pole exponential and its transform
t^{n−1} e^{−at} u(t)/(n − 1)!, a > 0 ‖ 1.about: Each extra factor of t differentiates the spectrum (t x(t) ↔ j dX/dω), raising the power of (a + jω) by one; the (n − 1)! cancels the factors the derivatives bring down. Use it to invert repeated factors in a partial-fraction expansion. A common mistake is dropping the (n − 1)!, or raising t to n instead of n − 1.
assumptions: a > 0 so the transform exists

example.problem: Invert 1/(2 + jω)^{3} and evaluate it at t = 1 s.

1 − |t|/T for |t| < T, 0 else ‖ T sin^{2.title: Triangle pulse and its transform
1 − |t|/T for |t| < T, 0 else ‖ T sin^{2.about: A triangle is a rectangle of width T convolved with itself (scaled), so its spectrum is a sinc squared: never negative and falling as 1/ω².
assumptions: At ω = 0 take the limit: X(0) = T, the triangle's area
Zeros at ω = 2πk/T, k ≠ 0
related: the rectangle it is built from

example.problem: A triangle of height 1 and half-width T = 2 s. Find X(0) and X at ω = 1 rad/s.

a x(t) + b y(t) ‖ a X(jω) + b Y(jω).title: Linearity (Fourier transform property)
a x(t) + b y(t) ‖ a X(jω) + b Y(jω).about: The analysis integral is linear, so transforms add and scale. With the table it turns a sum of known signals into a sum of known transforms. A common mistake is applying it to a product: x(t)y(t) needs the convolution of the spectra.
assumptions: X(jω) and Y(jω) both exist
related: y(t) = x(t) p(t) ↔ Y(jω) = (1/2π) X(jω) ∗ P(jω)
products are not term by term

example.problem: Find X(j2) for x(t) = 3e^{−2t}u(t) + 2δ(t).

x^{*}(t) ‖ X^{*}(−jω).title: Conjugation (Fourier transform property)
x^{*}(t) ‖ X^{*}(−jω).about: Conjugate the analysis integral: e^{−jωt} becomes e^{+jωt} = e^{−j(−ω)t}, hence the mirror in ω. For a real x, x = x^{*} gives X(−jω) = X^{*}(jω): the magnitude is even and the phase odd, so a one-sided plot says everything. A common mistake is thinking a real x has a real X; only a real, even x does.
assumptions: X(jω) exists
related: the series version for real x

example.problem: x(t) = e^{−t}u(t) is real, with X(j2) = 1/(1 + 2j) = 0.2 − 0.4j. Find X(−j2).

a^{|n|}, |a| < 1 ‖ (1 − a^{2})/(1 − 2a c.title: Two-sided geometric sequence and its DTFT
a^{|n|}, |a| < 1 ‖ (1 − a^{2})/(1 − 2a c.about: It is a^{n}u[n] plus its mirror a^{−n}u[−n], less the δ[n] counted twice: 1/(1 − ae^{−jω}) + 1/(1 − ae^{jω}) − 1 simplifies to this. Symmetric, so its DTFT is real and even; the discrete twin of e^{−a|t|}. A common mistake is forgetting to subtract the doubled n = 0 sample.
assumptions: |a| < 1 for convergence

example.problem: Find X(e^{j0}) for a = 0.5, and check it against the sum.

Σ_{k=−∞}^{∞} δ[n − kN] ‖ (2π/N) Σ_{k=−∞}.title: Discrete impulse train and its DTFT
Σ_{k=−∞}^{∞} δ[n − kN] ‖ (2π/N) Σ_{k=−∞}.about: A unit sample every N samples has N equal Fourier series coefficients 1/N, so its DTFT is impulses of area 2π/N every 2π/N. A common mistake is giving the impulses area 1/N: that is the series coefficient, and the DTFT carries 2π times it.
assumptions: N a positive integer
Generalised transform

example.problem: How many impulses fall in −π < ω ≤ π for N = 4?

a x[n] + b y[n] ‖ a X(e^{jω}) + b Y(e^{j.title: Linearity (DTFT property)
a x[n] + b y[n] ‖ a X(e^{jω}) + b Y(e^{j.about: The DTFT sum is linear, so transforms add and scale term by term; build a sequence's spectrum from table entries. A common mistake is applying it to a product: x[n]y[n] needs the periodic convolution of the spectra.
assumptions: Both DTFTs exist

example.problem: Find the DTFT of 2δ[n] − δ[n − 1] and its value at ω = π.

x^{*}[n] ‖ X^{*}(e^{−jω}).title: Conjugation (DTFT property)
x^{*}[n] ‖ X^{*}(e^{−jω}).about: Conjugating the DTFT sum turns e^{−jωn} into e^{+jωn} = e^{−j(−ω)n}, hence the mirror in ω. For a real x the magnitude is even and the phase odd, so 0 ≤ ω ≤ π says everything. A common mistake is thinking a real x has a real X; only a real, even x does.
assumptions: X(e^{jω}) exists

Σ_{k=−∞}^{n} x[k] ‖ X(e^{jω})/(1 − e^{−j.title: Accumulation (DTFT property)
Σ_{k=−∞}^{n} x[k] ‖ X(e^{jω})/(1 − e^{−j.about: The running sum is x convolved with u[n], so its DTFT is X times the step's DTFT. The impulse carries the DC part; it repeats every 2π. A common mistake is dropping the impulse when Σ x[n] ≠ 0.
assumptions: The impulse πX(e^{j0})δ(ω) repeats at every multiple of 2π; the table shows one period
It vanishes when X(e^{j0}) = Σ x[n] = 0
vars: DC value of X, Σ x[n]

example.problem: Find the DTFT of the running sum of 0.5^{n}u[n] at ω = π/2 (no impulse there).
steps: Y = X/(1 − e^{−jω}) away from ω = 0

Bins ‖ f_{k} = k f_{s}/N.title: DFT bin frequencies
Bins ‖ f_{k} = k f_{s}/N.about: Bin k of an N-point DFT samples the DTFT at ω = 2πk/N rad/sample, which is k f_{s}/N hertz, so bins are f_{s}/N apart (the resolution). A common mistake is reading bins above N/2 as high frequencies: they are the negative frequencies (k − N) f_{s}/N.
assumptions: N samples taken at f_{s}
Finer resolution needs a longer record (larger N at the same f_{s}), not zero-padding

example.problem: A 1024-point FFT at 48 kHz: what frequency is bin 100, and how far apart are bins?

cos(2A) = 2 cos^{2}(A) − 1 = 1 − 2 sin^{.title: Double angle for cosine, other forms
cos(2A) = 2 cos^{2}(A) − 1 = 1 − 2 sin^{.about: Swapping sin² for 1 − cos² (or the reverse) in cos(2A) = cos²A − sin²A gives forms with one function only. Use them to get cos 2A from cos A or sin A alone, and rearranged they are the power-reduction formulas.
assumptions: Any A, radians or degrees

example.problem: If cos A = 0.6, find cos 2A.

cos(A) + cos(B) = 2 cos((A + B)/2) cos((.title: Sum to product: beats
cos(A) + cos(B) = 2 cos((A + B)/2) cos((.about: A sum of two cosines is a product: a cosine at the average frequency times one at half the difference. Two close tones therefore sound as one tone whose loudness swells and fades, beats, at the difference frequency.
assumptions: Any A, B
Similarly cos A − cos B = −2 sin((A + B)/2) sin((A − B)/2)
The beat frequency is f₁ − f₂, twice the envelope's cosine frequency, since |cos| repeats twice per cycle

example.problem: Two tones at 440 Hz and 444 Hz play together. What is the beat frequency?
steps: The envelope |cos(2π·2t)| peaks 4 times a second

cosh^{2}(x) − sinh^{2}(x) = 1.title: Hyperbolic Pythagorean identity
cosh^{2}(x) − sinh^{2}(x) = 1.about: The hyperbolic version of sin² + cos² = 1, with a minus sign: (cosh x, sinh x) lies on the hyperbola X² − Y² = 1 as (cos x, sin x) lies on the circle. Use it to simplify and in substitutions like x = a sinh u.
assumptions: All real x
Follows from cosh x = (e^{x} + e^{−x})/2, sinh x = (e^{x} − e^{−x})/2

example.problem: Check it at x = 1.

j^{3} = −j, j^{4} = 1.title: Powers of j
j^{3} = −j, j^{4} = 1.about: Powers of the imaginary unit cycle through j, −1, −j, 1 every four steps, since each multiplication by j turns a quarter turn. So jⁿ depends only on n mod 4.
assumptions: n an integer; negative powers too: j^{−1} = −j
j and i are the same number

example.problem: Simplify j^{27}.

x(t) = (4A/π) Σ_{k=1,3,5,…} sin(kω_{o}t).title: Fourier series of a square wave
x(t) = (4A/π) Σ_{k=1,3,5,…} sin(kω_{o}t).about: A square wave that is +A for half a period and −A for the other half is odd and has half-wave symmetry, so only odd sine harmonics appear, falling off as 1/k. Use it straight away for "find the Fourier series of a square wave" or the power in its harmonics. Near each jump the partial sums overshoot by about 9% (Gibbs).
assumptions: x = +A for 0 < t < T/2 and −A for −T/2 < t < 0 (odd about t = 0)
A 0-to-A wave is A/2 plus half this series
Shifted by T/4 it becomes even: the sines turn into cosines with alternating signs

example.problem: A ±5 V square wave has period 2 ms. Find the amplitude and frequency of its third harmonic.
steps: f_{o} = 1/T = 500 Hz, so the third harmonic is at 1500 Hz

a_{k} = sin(kω_{o}T_{1})/(kπ).title: Fourier coefficients of a periodic pulse train
a_{k} = sin(kω_{o}T_{1})/(kπ).about: A train of unit-height rectangular pulses, each 2T_{1} wide and centred on t = 0, repeating every T. Its coefficients follow a sinc envelope; the duty cycle 2T_{1}/T sets where the zeros fall. This is the Oppenheim table entry for the "periodic square wave".
assumptions: Pulse height 1; for height A multiply every a_{k} by A
k ≠ 0; a_{0} = 2T_{1}/T, the duty cycle
Centred on t = 0 (even), so a_{k} is real
related: the single pulse: a_k is its transform sampled at kω_o, over T

example.problem: Unit pulses 2 µs wide repeat every 8 µs (25% duty). Find a_{0} and a_{1}.

x(t) = (8A/π^{2}) Σ_{k=1,3,5,…} cos(kω_{.title: Fourier series of a triangle wave
x(t) = (8A/π^{2}) Σ_{k=1,3,5,…} cos(kω_{.about: A triangle wave peaking at +A at t = 0 and −A at t = ±T/2 is even with half-wave symmetry: odd cosine harmonics only, falling as 1/k^{2}, so it converges much faster than a square wave (it has no jumps). It is the integral of a square wave.
assumptions: Peak +A at t = 0 (even); shifted by T/4 it becomes odd with sines
Zero average

example.problem: A ±2 V triangle wave. Find the amplitude of its third harmonic.

x(t) = (2A/π) Σ_{k=1}^{∞} (−1)^{k+1} sin.title: Fourier series of a sawtooth wave
x(t) = (2A/π) Σ_{k=1}^{∞} (−1)^{k+1} sin.about: A sawtooth rising linearly from −A to A over one period, then dropping, is odd: sine terms at every harmonic, alternating in sign and falling as 1/k. The jump makes it converge slowly with Gibbs overshoot.
assumptions: x = A t/(T/2) for −T/2 < t < T/2, repeated
Zero average
related: integrate by parts to get it

example.problem: Find the coefficient of sin(2ω_{o}t) for a sawtooth with A = 1.

a_{k} = 1/T.title: Fourier coefficients of an impulse train
a_{k} = 1/T.about: The periodic impulse train Σ δ(t − nT) has every coefficient equal to 1/T: all harmonics, equally strong. It is the sampling function, and its transform is another impulse train.
assumptions: Unit-area impulses every T
related: only the impulse at t = 0 lies in one period

example.problem: Impulses every 1 ms. Find a_{k}.
example.answer: a_{k} = 1000 s^{−1} (1/T, read as 1000 Hz) for every k

LTI ‖ b_{k} = a_{k} H(jkω_{o}).title: Fourier series through an LTI system
LTI ‖ b_{k} = a_{k} H(jkω_{o}).about: A periodic input to a stable LTI system gives a periodic output with the same ω_{o}; each harmonic is multiplied by the frequency response at its own frequency. This is how to find a filtered square wave, or which harmonics survive a filter.
assumptions: System LTI and stable; steady state (transients have died out)
H(jω) is the frequency response, the CTFT of h(t)

example.problem: A ±1 square wave (a_{1} = 2/(jπ)) drives an RC low-pass H = 1/(1 + jω/ω_{c}) with ω_{c} = ω_{o}. Find |b_{1}|.

Response ‖ H(jω) = Y(jω)/X(jω) = (Σ b_{k.title: Frequency response from a differential equation
Response ‖ H(jω) = Y(jω)/X(jω) = (Σ b_{k.about: Transform both sides of a linear constant-coefficient ODE: each d^{k}/dt^{k} becomes (jω)^{k}, so H(jω) is a ratio of polynomials in jω. Use it to get |H| and ∠H at a frequency, or h(t) by partial fractions.
assumptions: System LTI and stable (otherwise the CTFT of h may not exist)
Initial rest
vars: output and input coefficients of the ODE

example.problem: dy/dt + 2y = x(t). Find |H(jω)| at ω = 2 rad/s.

Sinusoid ‖ y(t) = |H(jω_{o})| cos(ω_{o}t.title: Sinusoidal steady-state output of an LTI system
Sinusoid ‖ y(t) = |H(jω_{o})| cos(ω_{o}t.about: A sinusoid into a stable LTI system comes out as the same-frequency sinusoid, scaled by |H| and shifted by ∠H at that frequency. It is the fastest route for "find y(t) for x(t) = cos(ω_{o}t)".
assumptions: Stable LTI, steady state
Real h(t), so H(−jω) = H^{*}(jω)

example.problem: H(jω) = 1/(1 + jω), input cos(t). Find y(t).

e^{−at} cos(ω_{o}t) u(t), a > 0 ‖ (a + j.title: CT Fourier pair: damped cosine
e^{−at} cos(ω_{o}t) u(t), a > 0 ‖ (a + j.about: A decaying cosine (an underdamped response) transforms to a resonant peak near ω = ±ω_{o} whose width is set by a. Replace s by jω in the Laplace pair to get it.
assumptions: a > 0, so the signal decays and the transform exists

example.problem: Find X(j0), the area under e^{−t} cos(2t) u(t).

e^{−at} sin(ω_{o}t) u(t), a > 0 ‖ ω_{o}/.title: CT Fourier pair: damped sine
e^{−at} sin(ω_{o}t) u(t), a > 0 ‖ ω_{o}/.about: A decaying sine, the impulse response of an underdamped second-order system, transforms to a resonant peak near ±ω_{o}.

example.problem: Find X(j0), the area under e^{−t} sin(2t) u(t).

x(t) cos(ω_{o}t) ‖ (1/2)[X(j(ω − ω_{o})).title: Modulation property (AM)
x(t) cos(ω_{o}t) ‖ (1/2)[X(j(ω − ω_{o})).about: Multiplying by a cosine carrier moves the spectrum to ±ω_{o}, each copy at half height. It is amplitude modulation, and demodulating (multiplying by the carrier again) puts a half-height copy back at 0 and copies at ±2ω_{o}.
assumptions: Copies do not overlap if ω_{o} exceeds the bandwidth of x

example.problem: A message band-limited to 5 kHz multiplies a 100 kHz carrier. Which band does the upper copy fill?
steps: The copy at +100 kHz spans 100 ± 5 kHz, at half height

x(t) Σ_{n} δ(t − nT) ‖ (1/T) Σ_{k} X(j(ω.title: Impulse sampling in frequency
x(t) Σ_{n} δ(t − nT) ‖ (1/T) Σ_{k} X(j(ω.about: Sampling with an impulse train repeats the spectrum every ω_{s} = 2π/T, scaled by 1/T. If x is band-limited below ω_{s}/2 the copies do not overlap and a low-pass filter recovers x (the sampling theorem); otherwise they overlap: aliasing.
assumptions: Ideal impulse sampling; real samplers hold, adding a sinc droop
related: the DT frequency of a sampled signal

example.problem: x is band-limited to 4 kHz and sampled at 10 kHz. Where does the first copy above the original begin?
steps: Copies are centred on 0, ±10 kHz, ±20 kHz, …
the one at 10 kHz reaches down to 10 − 4 kHz
example.answer: at 6 kHz: a 2 kHz guard band, no aliasing

Response ‖ H(e^{jω}) = (Σ b_{k} e^{−jωk}.title: Frequency response from a difference equation
Response ‖ H(e^{jω}) = (Σ b_{k} e^{−jωk}.about: Transform a linear constant-coefficient difference equation: each delay of k samples becomes e^{−jωk}, so H(e^{jω}) is a ratio of polynomials in e^{−jω}. With every a_{k} = 0 for k ≥ 1 it is an FIR filter: H is just Σ b_{k} e^{−jωk}.
assumptions: Stable LTI system; H repeats every 2π
ω = 0 is DC, ω = π is the highest frequency

example.problem: y[n] − 0.5 y[n − 1] = x[n]. Find |H| at ω = π.

Sampling ‖ ω = ΩT = 2πf/f_{s}.title: Discrete-time frequency of a sampled signal
Sampling ‖ ω = ΩT = 2πf/f_{s}.about: Sampling a CT sinusoid at f_{s} gives a DT sinusoid with frequency ω = ΩT radians per sample. ω = π is the Nyquist frequency f_{s}/2; anything above folds back (aliases).
assumptions: Unique only for |ω| ≤ π; higher f aliases to ω − 2πk

example.problem: A 1 kHz tone is sampled at 8 kHz. What is ω?

1 for 0 ≤ n ≤ N − 1, 0 else ‖ e^{−jω(N−1.title: DTFT of a rectangular window
1 for 0 ≤ n ≤ N − 1, 0 else ‖ e^{−jω(N−1.about: The length-N window starting at n = 0, the one used to truncate data. Its DTFT is a periodic sinc (Dirichlet kernel) with height N at ω = 0, first zeros at ±2π/N, and a linear phase from the (N − 1)/2 delay. Windowing a signal convolves its spectrum with this, which smears peaks (leakage).
assumptions: Sum of a finite geometric series: Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} e^{−jωn}
related: the centred window, no phase term

example.problem: An 8-point rectangular window. Find its peak and the width to its first zero.
steps: first zero where ωN/2 = π: ω = 2π/8
example.answer: peak 8, first zero at ω ≈ 0.7854 rad/sample

x[n] cos(ω_{o}n) ‖ (1/2)[X(e^{j(ω − ω_{o.title: DT modulation: a windowed cosine
x[n] cos(ω_{o}n) ‖ (1/2)[X(e^{j(ω − ω_{o.about: Multiplying by cos(ω_{o}n) shifts the spectrum to ±ω_{o} at half height. Read the other way, a cosine seen through a window w[n] has DTFT ½W centred on ±ω_{o}: that is the "DTFT of a windowed sinusoid" problem.
assumptions: Every spectrum repeats each 2π
related: 1 for 0 ≤ n ≤ N − 1, 0 else ↔ e^{−jω(N−1)/2} sin(ωN/2)/sin(ω/2)

example.problem: cos(πn/2) is kept for 0 ≤ n ≤ 7. How tall are the DTFT peaks at ±π/2?
steps: each peak is 8/2 (the other copy adds a little at that point)

x[n/k] if k divides n, 0 else ‖ X(e^{jkω.title: Time expansion (upsampling)
x[n/k] if k divides n, 0 else ‖ X(e^{jkω.about: Inserting k − 1 zeros between samples squeezes the spectrum by k, so k copies (images) of it appear in each 2π. An interpolation low-pass filter with cutoff π/k then removes the images.
assumptions: k a positive integer

example.problem: x has its band edge at ω = 0.4π. After upsampling by 2, where is the edge?
steps: X(e^{j2ω}): the edge moves to 0.4π/2, and an image appears around π

Samples ‖ X[k] = X(e^{j2πk/N}).title: The DFT samples the DTFT
Samples ‖ X[k] = X(e^{j2πk/N}).about: For x of length at most N, the N-point DFT is the DTFT sampled at N even frequencies ω_{k} = 2πk/N. Zero padding (a larger N) samples the same DTFT more finely but adds no resolution; only a longer record does.
assumptions: x[n] = 0 outside 0 ≤ n ≤ N − 1

example.problem: 64 samples at 1 kHz are zero padded to a 256-point FFT. What is the bin spacing?
